items.prompt: What is fault injection, per L1?
choices: Deliberately forcing a dependency to fail in a controlled test, instead of only testing what happens when it succeeds
A technique for finding syntax errors in test files
A way to automatically fix bugs found by a coverage report
A method for speeding up slow test suites by skipping some tests
items.explanation: Fault injection is specifically about forcing a dependency to fail on purpose, in a controlled test, to see how the system under test handles it — not a general-purpose speed or bug-fixing tool.
items.reference:
Tests covered
happy path, validation, business logic
Tests never covered
timeout, 500, connection refused, slow response

Why: fault injection exists specifically to fill the right-hand column on purpose, in a test, before it happens in production.

items.prompt: What question does fault injection answer that a coverage percentage can't, per L1?
choices: Not 'did this line run' but 'does the system survive when a dependency it calls doesn't behave'
Whether every function in the codebase has a docstring
Whether the test suite runs faster than a fixed time budget
Whether every variable name follows the team's style guide
items.explanation: L1's Scenario shows 100% coverage — every line ran — while the exact failure scenario that took the service down was never constructed as a test case. Coverage measures which lines ran, not which real-world failure scenarios were exercised.
items.reference:
Tests covered
happy path, validation, business logic
Tests never covered
timeout, 500, connection refused, slow response

Why: fault injection exists specifically to fill the right-hand column on purpose, in a test, before it happens in production.

items.prompt: Per L1, why isn't testing a validation error (like an empty cart) the same as fault injection?
choices: A validation error is bad input the code itself rejects on purpose; fault injection is about a dependency failing, not bad input
Validation errors and fault injection are actually the exact same thing under a different name
Fault injection only applies to database calls, never to input validation
Validation errors can only be tested manually, never in an automated suite
items.explanation: Validation-error tests exercise code paths the application itself controls and intentionally rejects. Fault injection exercises what happens when something outside the application's control — a dependency — misbehaves.
items.reference:
Tests covered
happy path, validation, business logic
Tests never covered
timeout, 500, connection refused, slow response

Why: fault injection exists specifically to fill the right-hand column on purpose, in a test, before it happens in production.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, why didn't 100% test coverage catch the outage before it shipped?
choices: Coverage measures which lines ran, and every line ran in testing — but the scenario of the dependency hanging was never constructed as a test case
The coverage tool had a bug and reported a false number
The tests were run on the wrong branch before merging
Coverage tools cannot measure network-related code at all
items.explanation: The network call's code ran during tests, so it counted toward coverage. What never ran was the pricing API actually hanging — coverage has no concept of which real-world failure scenarios were exercised, only which lines were.
items.reference:
✅ 100% coverage, all tests green
🐛 Outage caused by a scenario coverage can't see: a hung dependency

Why: coverage answers 'did this line run,' never 'did we test what happens when a dependency fails.'

items.prompt: What was the actual root cause of the checkout outage in L1's Scenario?
choices: The network call to the pricing API had no timeout, so the code waited forever for a response that never came
A discount calculation had an off-by-one bug
The database ran out of disk space
A validation check incorrectly rejected valid credit cards
items.explanation: No line of business logic was wrong. The bug was an absence — there was no bound on how long the checkout service was willing to wait for the pricing API to respond.
items.reference:
✅ 100% coverage, all tests green
🐛 Outage caused by a scenario coverage can't see: a hung dependency

Why: coverage answers 'did this line run,' never 'did we test what happens when a dependency fails.'

items.prompt: Per L1, what immediate effect did the hung pricing calls have on the rest of the checkout service?
choices: Every connection in the pool got stuck waiting on the pricing API, so new checkout requests couldn't get a connection at all
The service automatically restarted itself and recovered within seconds
Only the specific requests that called the pricing API were affected, everything else stayed fine
The pricing API's failure had no effect on checkout at all
items.explanation: The failure cascaded: because every connection ended up stuck waiting on a dependency that would never respond, the whole service lost the ability to serve new requests — not just the ones that needed a price.
items.reference:
✅ 100% coverage, all tests green
🐛 Outage caused by a scenario coverage can't see: a hung dependency

Why: coverage answers 'did this line run,' never 'did we test what happens when a dependency fails.'

items.prompt: Which of these does L1 name as a failure mode fault injection targets?
choices: A dependency that times out, returns an error, refuses the connection, or responds unusually slowly
A syntax error in the code under test itself
A test that fails randomly due to shared mutable state between tests
A missing import statement in the test file
items.explanation: L1 lists timeout/hang, error response, connection refused, and slow response as the failure modes fault injection targets — all dependency-side, not code-authoring mistakes or test hygiene issues.
items.reference:
Tests covered
happy path, validation, business logic
Tests never covered
timeout, 500, connection refused, slow response

Why: naming the failure modes precisely is what makes them writable as concrete tests.

items.prompt: Per L1, what distinguishes a dependency failure mode from an ordinary validation error test?
choices: A failure mode is the dependency misbehaving; a validation error is bad input the application itself rejects on purpose
There is no meaningful difference between the two
A failure mode always crashes the process, while a validation error never does
Validation errors can only be exercised through the UI, never through automated tests
items.explanation: The distinction is about where the failure originates: validation logic is code the application owns and controls; a dependency's failure is entirely outside the application's control, which is exactly why it needs to be simulated on purpose to test against.
items.reference:
Tests covered
happy path, validation, business logic
Tests never covered
timeout, 500, connection refused, slow response

Why: naming the failure modes precisely is what makes them writable as concrete tests.

items.prompt: Per L1, what does 'graceful degradation' mean?
choices: The system notices a dependency failed and does something sensible about it — retry, fallback, circuit-break, or a clear error — instead of hanging, crashing, or corrupting data
The system silently ignores any dependency that fails and continues as if nothing happened
The system always retries a failed call exactly once before giving up
The system logs the failure but takes no other action of any kind
items.explanation: Graceful degradation is a specific, observable set of behaviors — retry, fallback, circuit-break, or a clear error — not a vague notion of 'handling it somehow.'
items.reference:
✅ Graceful: retry, fallback, circuit-break, clear error
❌ Broken: hang, crash, silent corruption, cascade

Why: these are the two branches L2 formalizes as a diagram — one contains the failure, the other spreads or hides it.

items.prompt: Which of these, per L1, is an example of graceful degradation?
choices: Falling back to a cached or default value when a dependency fails
Waiting indefinitely for the dependency to eventually respond
Crashing the process the moment any dependency call fails
Returning subtly wrong data without indicating anything went wrong
items.explanation: Falling back to a cached or default value is one of the graceful behaviors L1 names, alongside retry, circuit-breaking, and surfacing a clear error — the other three options are exactly the broken behaviors L1 contrasts it with.
items.reference:
✅ Graceful: retry, fallback, circuit-break, clear error
❌ Broken: hang, crash, silent corruption, cascade

Why: these are the two branches L2 formalizes as a diagram — one contains the failure, the other spreads or hides it.

items.prompt: Which of these is a broken response to a failing dependency, per L1?
choices: Hanging indefinitely while holding a connection open, waiting for a response that will never come
Opening a circuit breaker after repeated failures
Surfacing a clear, typed error to the caller
Retrying the call a bounded number of times with backoff
items.explanation: Hanging indefinitely is exactly the broken behavior from L1's Scenario — it holds a resource open forever instead of failing in a bounded, visible way, unlike the other three options which are all graceful.
items.reference:
✅ Graceful: retry, fallback, circuit-break, clear error
❌ Broken: hang, crash, silent corruption, cascade

Why: these are the two branches L2 formalizes as a diagram — one contains the failure, the other spreads or hides it.

items.prompt: Per L1, how does fault injection relate to test doubles (mocks/stubs/fakes)?
choices: It often reuses the same seam a test double uses to swap out a dependency, but points it at making the dependency fail instead of succeed
Fault injection and test doubles are entirely unrelated techniques with no shared mechanism
Fault injection replaces test doubles entirely and makes them unnecessary
Test doubles can only ever simulate success, and fault injection is a completely different mechanism unrelated to seams
items.explanation: L1 is explicit: fault injection reuses the same injection seam test doubles use, but the goal is different — simulating failure instead of a normal, successful response.
items.reference:
🔌 Same seam — the point where a dependency can be swapped
🎯 Different goal — success double vs. failure double

Why: the mechanism (swap what's behind the seam) is identical; only what gets put there differs.

items.prompt: Per L1, is fault injection a replacement for using test doubles to isolate a test from a slow dependency?
choices: No — they serve different goals even though they can share the same seam in the code
Yes — fault injection makes test doubles for isolation obsolete
Yes, but only for tests written in JavaScript
No — because fault injection never uses seams of any kind
items.explanation: A test double for isolation and a fault-injection double both live at the same seam, but they answer different questions — one isolates from a real dependency to run fast and predictably; the other deliberately breaks that dependency to see what the caller does.
items.reference:
🔌 Same seam — the point where a dependency can be swapped
🎯 Different goal — success double vs. failure double

Why: the mechanism (swap what's behind the seam) is identical; only what gets put there differs.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does injecting a timeout/hang fault test for?
choices: Whether the caller has a timeout of its own, or waits forever
Whether the caller correctly formats its own request
Whether the dependency's database is properly indexed
Whether the caller's UI renders a loading spinner
items.explanation: A timeout/hang fault specifically exercises whether the caller bounds how long it's willing to wait — a code path that a success-only test suite never touches.
items.reference:
Timeout/hangdoes the caller time out, or wait forever?
Error responsedoes the caller check status, or trust any response?
Malformed bodydoes the caller validate shape, or trust it blindly?

Why: each fault type exercises a different piece of defensive code — one check rarely protects against all of them.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does injecting an error-response fault (like a 500) test for, that a timeout fault doesn't?
choices: Whether the caller checks the response status, rather than trusting any response it gets
Whether the caller has a network connection at all
Whether the dependency's server has enough disk space
Whether the caller's retry logic uses exponential backoff
items.explanation: An error response actually arrives — the question is whether the caller inspects its status before trusting the body. A timeout fault, by contrast, tests whether the caller bounds its wait, since no response arrives at all.
items.reference:
Timeout/hangdoes the caller time out, or wait forever?
Error responsedoes the caller check status, or trust any response?
Malformed bodydoes the caller validate shape, or trust it blindly?

Why: each fault type exercises a different piece of defensive code — one check rarely protects against all of them.

items.prompt: Per L2's Checkpoint, a caller does `if (!response.ok) throw`. Does that check protect it against a pure timeout/hang?
choices: No — there's no response yet to check `.ok` on when the call is still pending
Yes — that check protects against every fault type in L2's table
Yes, because `.ok` is `false` by default while a call is pending
No, because that check doesn't work for any fault type at all
items.explanation: A timeout means the call never resolves at all — there's no response object yet for `.ok` to be checked on. That check only protects against the error-response row, not a hang.
items.reference:
Timeout/hangdoes the caller time out, or wait forever?
Error responsedoes the caller check status, or trust any response?
Malformed bodydoes the caller validate shape, or trust it blindly?

Why: each fault type exercises a different piece of defensive code — one check rarely protects against all of them.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what do all four 'graceful' outcomes have in common?
choices: The failure stays contained — visible, bounded in time, and doesn't take anything else down with it
They all involve retrying the failed call at least three times
They all avoid logging the failure to keep logs clean
They all require a human to intervene manually before the system recovers
items.explanation: Retry, fallback, circuit-break, and clear error all share one property regardless of which specific behavior is used: the failure is contained rather than left open-ended or hidden.
items.reference:
✅ Graceful — contained: visible, bounded, doesn't spread
❌ Broken — spreads or hides: unbounded, silent, or cascading

Why: naming the shared property is what makes 'graceful' a testable assertion, not a vibe.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what do all four 'broken' outcomes have in common?
choices: The failure spreads or hides — it holds resources indefinitely, stops the process, hides behind wrong data, or drags unrelated requests down too
They all happen only when the dependency is completely offline
They all cause the test suite itself to fail immediately
They only occur in systems written in dynamically typed languages
items.explanation: Hang, crash, silent corruption, and cascading failure look different on the surface but share the same underlying shape: the failure is not contained — it either never ends, takes the whole process down, lies about succeeding, or spreads to unrelated work.
items.reference:
✅ Graceful — contained: visible, bounded, doesn't spread
❌ Broken — spreads or hides: unbounded, silent, or cascading

Why: naming the shared property is what makes 'graceful' a testable assertion, not a vibe.

items.prompt: Per L2's Checkpoint, a service retries a failed call 5 times with no delay between attempts, then gives up. Is that fully graceful degradation?
choices: Only partially — it retries and gives up cleanly rather than hanging, but retrying with no backoff adds load to an already-struggling dependency
Yes, completely — any retry-then-give-up behavior counts as fully graceful
No, not at all — retrying is always a broken response to a failure
It depends only on whether the retries succeed, not on their spacing
items.explanation: The shape is graceful (it doesn't hang forever), but the spacing isn't — a real retry needs backoff to avoid piling more load onto a dependency that's already failing, not just to eventually stop.
items.reference:
✅ Graceful — contained: visible, bounded, doesn't spread
❌ Broken — spreads or hides: unbounded, silent, or cascading

Why: naming the shared property is what makes 'graceful' a testable assertion, not a vibe.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, is a fault-injection test's failure intended?
choices: Yes — the test deliberately forces a dependency to fail, unlike a flaky test's unintended failure
No — fault-injection tests fail purely by accident, exactly like flaky tests
It depends on which testing framework is used
Neither flaky tests nor fault-injection tests ever fail intentionally
items.explanation: A fault-injection test's failure of the dependency is deliberate and controlled by the test itself — the whole point is to construct the failure on purpose, unlike a flaky test's accidental non-determinism.
items.reference:
Flaky testunintended, uncontrolled, undermines trust
Fault-injection testintended, controlled, builds trust

Why: both involve a test whose outcome touches timing or failure — but one is an accident to eliminate, the other a deliberate probe to keep.

items.prompt: Per L2, what does a flaky test do to trust in a suite, compared to a fault-injection test?
choices: A flaky test undermines trust since a red run might mean nothing; a fault-injection test's red run means a real gap was found
Both undermine trust in exactly the same way and to the same degree
A fault-injection test undermines trust more, since it fails on purpose
Neither type of test has any effect on trust in the suite
items.explanation: A flaky red run is ambiguous — it might be nothing. A fault-injection red run is meaningful by design: it means the system genuinely failed to handle a deliberately constructed failure scenario.
items.reference:
Flaky testunintended, uncontrolled, undermines trust
Fault-injection testintended, controlled, builds trust

Why: both involve a test whose outcome touches timing or failure — but one is an accident to eliminate, the other a deliberate probe to keep.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what is 'the fix' for a fault-injection test that reliably fails when a dependency hangs?
choices: Nothing needs fixing in the test itself — it's working as designed; the fix belongs in the code under test
Remove the fault-injection test entirely, since a reliably failing test is always a bug
Rewrite the test to always pass regardless of the dependency's behavior
Add a retry to the test itself until it happens to pass
items.explanation: Unlike a flaky test (whose fix is removing non-determinism from the test), a fault-injection test that reliably fails against a broken system is correct — the fix is in the system under test, not the test.
items.reference:
Flaky testunintended, uncontrolled, undermines trust
Fault-injection testintended, controlled, builds trust

Why: both involve a test whose outcome touches timing or failure — but one is an accident to eliminate, the other a deliberate probe to keep.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the difference between a test double used for isolation and a fault-injection double, given they sit at the same seam?
choices: One returns a normal successful response for speed and determinism; the other deliberately returns a failure to see what the caller does
A fault-injection double is always slower to write code for than a real dependency
There is no real difference — they are the exact same object used interchangeably
A test double for isolation can only be used once per test suite
items.explanation: Both live at the same swap point in the code, but what's put there differs by intent: a normal successful response for isolation, or a deliberate failure to probe the caller's failure-handling.
items.reference:
🔌 Same seam, different fill: success double vs. failure double
🚫 No seam at all → nothing to fault-inject, same limit as unit testing

Why: a codebase needs a seam before it can be fault-injection tested, exactly like it needs one before it can be unit tested with a double.

items.prompt: Per L2, can a codebase be fault-injection tested if it calls `fetch` directly, inline, with nothing swappable?
choices: No — it needs a seam created first, the same requirement test-doubles has for unit testing at all
Yes — fault injection works identically regardless of whether a seam exists
Yes, but only if the codebase is written in a statically typed language
No — fault injection is impossible for any HTTP-based dependency
items.explanation: Without a seam, there's nowhere to substitute a failure. This mirrors the same limitation test-doubles has: no swap point means no ability to control what the dependency does in a test, whether that's for isolation or for fault injection.
items.reference:
🔌 Same seam, different fill: success double vs. failure double
🚫 No seam at all → nothing to fault-inject, same limit as unit testing

Why: a codebase needs a seam before it can be fault-injection tested, exactly like it needs one before it can be unit tested with a double.

items.prompt: Per L2, what's the key difference between test-level fault injection and production chaos engineering?
choices: Fault injection forces a specific known failure mode in a controlled test before shipping; chaos engineering surfaces unknown failure modes in a live system
Fault injection only works in production, while chaos engineering only works in a test suite
There is no real difference — the two terms describe the exact same practice
Chaos engineering is only a marketing term with no distinct technique behind it
items.explanation: Fault injection here is a pre-ship, test-level technique targeting a known or suspected failure mode. Chaos engineering deliberately breaks a live system to find failure modes nobody predicted in advance.
items.reference:
🧪 Fault injection — known risk, test-level, before ship
🌪️ Chaos engineering — unknown risk, production, after ship

Why: neither replaces the other — they catch different kinds of risk at different stages of a system's life.

items.prompt: Per L2, does chaos engineering replace test-level fault injection, or the other way around?
choices: Neither replaces the other — they catch different kinds of risk at different stages
Chaos engineering fully replaces fault injection, making test-level fault injection unnecessary
Fault injection fully replaces chaos engineering, making production experiments unnecessary
They're the same practice, so the question of replacement doesn't apply
items.explanation: L2 is explicit that fault injection catches known risks before deploy, and chaos engineering finds unknown risks after — a team benefits from both, not one instead of the other.
items.reference:
🧪 Fault injection — known risk, test-level, before ship
🌪️ Chaos engineering — unknown risk, production, after ship

Why: neither replaces the other — they catch different kinds of risk at different stages of a system's life.

Timeout/hang — it already has a time limit on the network call
Connection refused — it retries automatically with backoff
Malformed body — it validates the shape of the price field

items.reference:
✅ Handles: non-ok status throws
❌ Missing: any bound on how long it waits

Why: a function can correctly handle one fault type from L2's table and still be completely exposed to another.

items.prompt: In L3's original `fetchPricing`, which fault type does it do nothing about?
choices: Timeout/hang — there's no time limit on `await pricingService.getPrice(productId)`
Error response — it never checks the response status at all
Malformed body — it never returns the price field to the caller
It handles every fault type from L2's table correctly

items.reference:
✅ Handles: non-ok status throws
❌ Missing: any bound on how long it waits

Why: a function can correctly handle one fault type from L2's table and still be completely exposed to another.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the fault-injection test need its own `withTestTimeout` guard, separate from the function under test?
choices: Because the function under test doesn't have a timeout yet — without the test's own guard, a hanging `fetchPricing` would hang the whole test run
Because JavaScript requires every test to have an explicit timeout by law of the language spec
Because the guard is what actually fixes the bug in `fetchPricing`
It doesn't need one — the test would resolve on its own regardless
items.explanation: Until the fix ships, nothing in `fetchPricing` bounds the wait, so the test needs its own independent guard to fail fast with a clear message instead of hanging the whole suite indefinitely.
items.reference:
🧪 Test's own guard — fails fast with a clear message
🔧 Function's timeout (the fix) — the actual behavior being verified

Why: a hanging dependency under test can't be allowed to hang the test suite itself.

items.prompt: Per L3, after the fix adds a 500ms timeout inside `fetchPricing`, what has to change about the test's own guard threshold?
choices: It must be raised above 500ms, or the test's guard would trip before `fetchPricing`'s own timeout even gets a chance to fire
It must be lowered below 500ms so the test finishes faster
Nothing changes — the guard's threshold is unrelated to the function's own timeout
The guard can be removed entirely once the fix ships
items.explanation: If the test's guard fires before the function's own 500ms timeout would, the test can no longer distinguish 'the function has a working timeout' from 'the test gave up first' — the guard has to leave room for the real timeout to actually run.
items.reference:
🧪 Test's own guard — fails fast with a clear message
🔧 Function's timeout (the fix) — the actual behavior being verified

Why: a hanging dependency under test can't be allowed to hang the test suite itself.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the actual difference in purpose between the test's own timeout guard and the fix's timeout inside `fetchPricing`?
choices: The test's guard exists so a failing test still reports a clear failure quickly; the function's timeout is the real behavior being verified
They serve the exact same purpose and either one alone would be sufficient
The test's guard is what makes checkout resilient in production, not the function's timeout
The function's timeout exists only to make the test file shorter
items.explanation: These are two different concerns even though both are 'timeouts': the test's guard is test infrastructure protecting the suite; the function's timeout is the production behavior the whole exercise exists to verify and fix.
items.reference:
🧪 Test's own guard — fails fast with a clear message
🔧 Function's timeout (the fix) — the actual behavior being verified

Why: a hanging dependency under test can't be allowed to hang the test suite itself.

items.prompt: Per L3, why can't every possible fault be injected in a test suite?
choices: The space of things that could go wrong with a dependency is unbounded, so faults have to be prioritized by likelihood and impact, like any other risk
Testing infrastructure technically cannot simulate more than one fault type per codebase
Fault injection tests are prohibited by most testing frameworks after the first one
Every fault type produces an identical test, so injecting more than one adds nothing
items.explanation: There's no ceiling on the number of ways a dependency could theoretically misbehave, so writing a fault-injection test for every conceivable one isn't realistic — prioritizing by likelihood and impact is the same judgment used for any risk.
items.reference:
⚖️ Prioritize by likelihood × impact, same as any risk
✅ Pricing API timeout under load — common AND high-impact

Why: a real one-in-a-billion malformed byte sequence is a weaker use of test-writing time than a fault that already caused a real outage.

items.prompt: Per L3, why is the pricing API timing out under load an easy case to prioritize a fault-injection test for?
choices: It's both common (real networks are sometimes slow) and high-impact (it already took down checkout in L1's Scenario)
Because it's the only fault type that can be tested without a mock
Because timeouts are always easier to code than error responses
Because it's the least likely of all the fault types, which makes it worth double-checking
items.explanation: L3 explicitly frames prioritization as likelihood times impact — a timeout under load scores high on both axes, unlike a hypothetical, never-observed malformed-byte scenario.
items.reference:
⚖️ Prioritize by likelihood × impact, same as any risk
✅ Pricing API timeout under load — common AND high-impact

Why: a real one-in-a-billion malformed byte sequence is a weaker use of test-writing time than a fault that already caused a real outage.

🌪️ Chaos engineering — finds the next gap, in a live system

🌪️ Chaos engineering — finds the next gap, in a live system

items.prompt: Complete classifyFault(response) so it classifies a synthetic dependency response into one of L2's fault types. `response === null` means a timeout/hang (no response at all). `response.refused === true` means connection refused. `!response.ok` means an error response. A `response.ok` with no `response.body` or a non-number `response.body.price` means a malformed body. Anything else returns "ok".

tests.description: ok with a non-number price is malformed
ok with a valid numeric price is ok

items.explanation: Each check maps directly to one row of L2's fault-type table: no response at all is a timeout, a refused connection is its own category, a present-but-failing status is an error, and a present-but-wrong-shaped body is malformed -- everything else is a genuinely successful response.
items.reference:
nulltimeout
refused: trueconnection-refused
ok: falseerror
bad body shapemalformed

Why: naming the fault type first is what lets the caller decide the right graceful response for each one, per L2.

items.prompt: Same classifyFault(response) as before. Confirm your implementation correctly distinguishes a connection-refused response from a null (timeout) response, and correctly treats an ok response with an extra unrelated field as still "ok".

tests.description: an ok response with an extra field is still ok
tests.expr: expect(classifyFault({ ok: true, body: { price: 100, currency: "USD" } })).toBe("ok")

tests.description: missing body entirely on an ok response is malformed
a 404-style error is still classified as error, not malformed

items.explanation: An extra unrelated field never blocks a genuinely successful response from being classified as ok -- per L1's consumer-driven spirit, only the fields the caller actually depends on (here, a numeric price) matter to the check. A missing body or a non-2xx-style status are each their own distinct category, not interchangeable with each other.

Why: naming the fault type first is what lets the caller decide the right graceful response for each one, per L2.

items.prompt: Complete resolvePricing(outcome, cache, productId), mirroring L3's fixed fetchPricing but taking an already-computed `outcome` instead of a real async call. `outcome` is either `{ ok: true, price: N }` or `{ ok: false, reason: "..." }`. On success: call cache.set(productId, outcome.price) and return { price: outcome.price, stale: false }. On failure: if cache.get(productId) is not undefined, return { price: <cached>, stale: true }; otherwise throw new Error(`pricing unavailable for ${productId}: ${outcome.reason}`).

tests.description: a successful outcome caches the price and returns it fresh
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map(); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; return expect(resolvePricing({ ok: true, price: 4999 }, cache, "sku-1")).toEqual({ price: 4999, stale: false }); })()

tests.description: a failing outcome with a cached price falls back, marked stale
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([["sku-1", 4500]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; return expect(resolvePricing({ ok: false, reason: "timeout" }, cache, "sku-1")).toEqual({ price: 4500, stale: true }); })()

tests.description: a failing outcome with no cached price throws a clear error
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map(); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; return expect(() => resolvePricing({ ok: false, reason: "timeout" }, cache, "sku-9")).toThrow(); })()

items.explanation: This is the exact decision tree from L3's fixed fetchPricing, minus the real network call and timeout race -- a success caches and returns fresh, a failure with a cache hit falls back and flags stale, and a failure with no cache hit is the one case where a clear thrown error is the right graceful outcome, per L2's table.
items.reference:
✅ Success → cache it, return fresh
🕰️ Failure + cache hit → return stale price
❌ Failure + no cache → clear thrown error

Why: this is the same graceful-degradation decision tree fetchPricing makes, isolated from the real timing so it can be tested directly.

items.prompt: Same resolvePricing(outcome, cache, productId) as before. Confirm a successful outcome overwrites any previously cached price for that product, and that a failure never touches the cache for an unrelated product id.

tests.description: a fresh success overwrites a stale cached value
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([["sku-1", 4000]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; resolvePricing({ ok: true, price: 5200 }, cache, "sku-1"); return expect(cache.get("sku-1")).toBe(5200); })()

tests.description: a failure never writes to the cache
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([["sku-1", 4000]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; resolvePricing({ ok: false, reason: "error" }, cache, "sku-1"); return expect(cache.get("sku-1")).toBe(4000); })()

tests.description: a failure for one product doesn't affect a different product's cached price
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([["sku-2", 999]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; try { resolvePricing({ ok: false, reason: "timeout" }, cache, "sku-1"); } catch (e) {} return expect(cache.get("sku-2")).toBe(999); })()

items.explanation: The cache is only ever written to on a genuine success, keyed per product id -- a failure reads from it (to look for a fallback) but never writes, and never touches any product id other than the one it was called for, which is exactly the isolation a real multi-product checkout depends on.
